clue.text: Awful pain, with a word of course that could be produced onstage, only put on by women.

definitions.text: could be produced onstage, only put on by women

indicators.note: something awful is in a bad state, so the letters of pain are thrown into a new order

parts.note: fore is the warning a golfer shouts on the golf course

explanation.surface: Someone in dreadful pain hears a shout on the golf course, then wanders into a theatre and a women's dress shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awful' turns PAIN into PINA. The definition plays on two things: HMS Pinafore is a Gilbert and Sullivan operetta staged in theatres, and a pinafore is an apron-like dress worn by women.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses fit: the operetta HMS Pinafore is staged, and the sleeveless garment is traditionally worn by girls and women.

clue.text: A character of The Mikado has a ship-wreck, and finally gets shut out.

indicators.note: a wreck is a ship broken up, so the letters of ship are scrambled
out here means disordered, so the letters of shut are rearranged

explanation.surface: A character from the operetta is shipwrecked and finally locked out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wreck' turns SHIP into PISH and 'out' turns SHUT into TUSH. The Mikado is a Gilbert and Sullivan comic opera set in Japan.
explanation.definitionFit: Pish-Tush is the noble lord in Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera.

clue.text: The man without a country, with no language to show it.

indicators.note: the two words show the name openly within them, across the gap between them

parts.note: the name sits in plain sight across these two words, the whole of 'no' and the start of 'language'

explanation.surface: A stateless man who does not even have a language to prove it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to show it' means the name is on display inside 'no language'. The Man Without a Country is Edward Everett Hale's 1863 story about Philip Nolan, an officer exiled at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip Nolan is the title character of Hale's story, condemned never to hear of his homeland again.

clue.text: Maybe starts with the first course, and ends up with the last–or is just a seafood dish in itself.

parts.note: in a formal dinner the fish course comes early
cakes come as dessert, the last course

explanation.surface: A dinner that opens with one course and closes with another, or is a whole dish alone.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue builds a meal running from fish to cakes, then says the two words together name one dish.
explanation.definitionFit: Fishcakes are patties of flaked fish and potato, fried: a seafood dish.

clue.text: Proving some of you guys out there are Reds, possibly.

definitions.text: some of you guys out there

indicators.note: possibly says these letters could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Evidence that some of the audience are Communists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges ARE and REDS together. The setter addresses the magazine's audience: you who read this are readers. 'Reds' looks like Communists, a pointed joke in The Nation.
explanation.definitionFit: The people out there working the puzzle are the magazine's readership.

clue.text: You shouldn't leave things hanging in such a fashion–being found in the central part of the tune.

definitions.text: You shouldn't leave things hanging in such a fashion

parts.note: mid means middle, the central part
an air is a tune or melody

explanation.surface: Advice against leaving matters unresolved, found somewhere in the middle of a melody.
explanation.walkthrough: Things left hanging in mid-air are left unsettled; the definition plays on the idiom and on things literally dangling.
explanation.definitionFit: To leave something in mid-air is the idiom for leaving it suspended and unresolved.

clue.text: I point around a disheveled bum to fill with color, inspiration, etc.

definitions.text: to fill with color, inspiration, etc.

indicators.note: around says the first pair of letters wraps the rearranged word

parts.note: I as written plus E, a compass point (east)

indicators.note: disheveled means untidy, so the letters of bum are messed up

explanation.surface: Someone points at a scruffy tramp in order to give him some colour and spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bum' is American slang for a tramp, and 'disheveled' gives MBU; 'point' is a compass point, east, which 'around' joins with I to wrap the scrambled word.
explanation.definitionFit: To imbue is to saturate or inspire, as with a dye or a feeling.

clue.text: Such as the aardvark show a way to toss in your chips, and stare in a nasty fashion.

parts.note: to ante is to put chips into the pot at poker

indicators.note: in a nasty fashion means stare gets mangled into a different order

explanation.surface: Aardvarks demonstrate how to bet at poker and glare unpleasantly.
explanation.walkthrough: In poker the ante is each player's stake before the deal; 'in a nasty fashion' gives ATERS. The aardvark is not a true anteater, hence 'such as'.
explanation.definitionFit: The aardvark feeds on ants and termites, so it is loosely classed among anteaters.

clue.text: What one does with the clock at both ends of the summer season, possibly.

definitions.text: What one does with the clock at both ends of the summer season, possibly

parts.words: What one does with the clock at both ends of the summer season, possibly
parts.note: daylight saving time means moving clocks forward in spring and back in autumn

explanation.walkthrough: At the start and end of daylight saving time, clocks are put forward or back by an hour.
explanation.definitionFit: Adjusting a clock's time is setting it again, which is what everyone does twice a year.

clue.text: The old model you rode in has a not-so-smooth finish–but it's a place to eat for the lower types.

definitions.text: a place to eat for the lower types

parts.words: The old model you rode in
parts.note: the Model T was Ford's early mass-produced car
a rough finish is one that is not smooth

explanation.surface: A classic car with scuffed paintwork, ending up at a cheap diner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the lower types' are animals such as pigs, which eat from a trough.
explanation.definitionFit: A trough is the long open container from which livestock feed.

clue.text: In place, is returning to the French, marking those ready to be called up.

indicators.note: returning means the word is is read backwards

parts.note: les is the French plural for the

parts.words: marking those ready to be called up
parts.note: 1-A is the US draft classification for men available for military service; 1 is read as the letter I

explanation.surface: Someone back in a French town is marked down as fit to be drafted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns IS into SI. The American Selective Service gave the label 1-A to men fit and available for call-up; reading the 1 as I gives IA.
explanation.definitionFit: Silesia is a historic region of central Europe, now mostly in Poland, so it is a place.

clue.text: Sales pitches prove to be wrong in what British homeowners pay.

indicators.note: in tells us the reshuffled pair of letters sits inside the tax word

parts.note: rates were the British local property tax paid by householders

indicators.note: wrong signals that the two letters of be are put in a different order

explanation.surface: Salesmen's patter turns out to be mistaken about what British householders owe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' gives EB, and 'in' sets it inside rates, Britain's local tax on homes until 1990. 'Pitches' means sales inducements, not football fields.
explanation.definitionFit: Rebates are refunds or discounts offered to buyers, a common sales inducement.

clue.text: At first the scale is supposed to be good for you, at the junction with a false coin.

definitions.text: supposed to be good for you

indicators.note: at first asks for only the opening letter of the next word

parts.note: first letter of the word the

indicators.note: a false coin is a fake, so the letters of coin are counterfeited into a new order

explanation.surface: A musical scale said to be healthy meets a counterfeit coin at a crossroads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At first' takes T from 'the', and 'false' turns COIN into ONIC; 'at the junction with' simply joins them. 'Scale' is a nod to the musical sense: the tonic is a scale's keynote.
explanation.definitionFit: A tonic is a medicine or drink taken to invigorate, believed to improve health.

clue.text: Wildly happy with the former spouse over in Germany, with a busy working type.

parts.note: an ex is a former husband or wife
über is the German word for over
the ant is the proverbially busy worker insect

explanation.surface: Someone thrilled to be in Germany with their ex and a hard-working colleague.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' looks like a direction, but read with 'in Germany' it asks for the German word for over.
explanation.definitionFit: Exuberant describes lively, overflowing high spirits, so it suits someone wildly happy.

clue.text: They take away what a live wire will give you, and get you over the bumpy parts.

definitions.text: They take away what a live wire will give you
definitions.meaning: first meaning: things that absorb ..., the jolt from a live electrical wire

definitions.text: get you over the bumpy parts
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the dampers on a car that smooth out bumps in the road

explanation.walkthrough: The first half reads the phrase literally, as anything that soaks up an electric shock; the second is the car part.
explanation.definitionFit: Shock absorbers are the suspension dampers of a vehicle, and the phrase literally names things that take in jolts.

clue.text: One hopes not to do it with the mark, and hovers around, also coming up.

definitions.text: One hopes not to do it with the mark

indicators.note: around here means turned about, so the letters of hovers are rearranged
in a down entry, coming up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: too means also

explanation.surface: An archer hoping to hit the target hovers about as it rises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' looks like a container word but is the anagram signal, giving OVERSH; 'coming up' turns 'too' upside down to 'oot', which works only in a down entry. 'The mark' is a target, as in 'wide of the mark'.
explanation.definitionFit: To overshoot the mark is to go past a target, which any marksman hopes to avoid.

clue.text: Such a boat could hold quite a bit of beer.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a sailing ship with two or more masts

definitions.text: could hold quite a bit of beer
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a tall beer glass, larger than a standard one in the US

explanation.walkthrough: The vessel and the glass share a name; the clue pretends a ship's hold is full of beer.
explanation.definitionFit: A schooner is both a fore-and-aft rigged sailing vessel and a large drinking glass for beer.

clue.text: Having lost your way, but not on the golf circuit!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: astray from the intended route
second meaning: literally off the golf course

explanation.walkthrough: 'But' and the exclamation mark join two readings of one phrase: astray, and away from the links.
explanation.definitionFit: Off course is the idiom for straying from a planned route; read literally it means away from a course.

clue.text: Not a very nice occasion, possibly associated with Greenwich during a spell of it.

definitions.note: a phrase standing for the noun, the interval while something else happens

parts.note: mean means unkind, not nice
a time is an occasion, as in 'that time we met'

explanation.surface: An unpleasant occasion somehow linked with the London borough of Greenwich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly associated with Greenwich' is an extra hint: Greenwich Mean Time is the world's time standard, kept at the observatory in Greenwich, London.
explanation.definitionFit: The meantime is the intervening period, and 'in the meantime' means meanwhile.

clue.text: They supposedly lead a low life, with vegetables being given to the workers.

definitions.text: They supposedly lead a low life

parts.note: peas are vegetables
worker ants are the crossword's standard workers

explanation.surface: Lowly folk are handed vegetables meant for the labourers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low life' is used in the sense of humble social station, not criminality.
explanation.definitionFit: Peasants were the poor agricultural labourers at the bottom of the social order.

clue.text: Had to have the answer!

parts.note: something one had to have is something one required; the exclamation suggests a solver desperate for the solution

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a frustrated solver; read plainly, 'had to have' is simply a past-tense verb of requirement.
explanation.definitionFit: If you had to have something, you required it: a plain past-tense synonym.

clue.text: Bring you and me up to the top of the church, for a long sigh.

definitions.note: a noun phrase standing for the verb to sigh deeply

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: us means you and me
a spire is the tapering top of a church tower

explanation.surface: Hauling the two of us up the church steeple would make anyone sigh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' gives SU only because this is a down entry. Suspire is a rare literary word, so the wordplay carries most of the load.
explanation.definitionFit: Suspire is a literary verb meaning to breathe out deeply, to sigh.

clue.text: Defensive ditch, holding a ship with the enemy about.

indicators.note: holding means one word contains the other, as a hand holds something
about says the enemy word goes round the outside of the ship letters

parts.note: a foe is an enemy
SS is the abbreviation for steamship

explanation.surface: A trench around a castle with an enemy vessel trapped in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding' and 'about' both say the enemy word wraps round the ship letters; it is the foe, not the ship, that is on the outside.
explanation.definitionFit: A fosse is a moat or trench dug as a fortification.

clue.text: A number with fruit being spotted.

parts.note: D is the Roman numeral for 500
an apple is a fruit

explanation.surface: A numbered piece of fruit has been noticed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spotted' looks like 'seen', but here it means marked with spots.
explanation.definitionFit: Dapple, used of a horse's coat, means marked with patches of a different shade.

clue.text: See 14
The outer sort of path to travel.

indicators.note: sort of hints that the letters of outer are only roughly in place and need rearranging

explanation.surface: An outer circuit to follow on a journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The outer sort of path' reads like a ring road; 'outer' is the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A route is the way or course taken to get from one place to another.

clue.text: Such a count could be a knockout, frequently.

definitions.text: Such a count could be a knockout
definitions.meaning: first meaning, split in two words: a referee's count to the number that ends a boxing bout

explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words, OF TEN: a count of ten over a fallen boxer is a knockout. Read as one word it means frequently.
explanation.definitionFit: Often is the everyday adverb for many times, and split it describes a boxing referee's full count.

clue.text: Classic letter that is crumpled about a certain point.

indicators.note: about places the rearranged word round the compass letter
crumpled means the word that is screwed up into another order

parts.note: E, east, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: An old letter is crumpled up around some particular spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crumpled' turns THAT into THTA, and 'about' puts it around E, a compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: Theta is the eighth letter of the Greek alphabet, the classical alphabet.

clue.text: Put on a play with vegetables, obviously in favor of the Italian leader.

parts.note: pro means in favour of
Il Duce, the leader, was Mussolini's title

explanation.surface: Staging a play with vegetables while openly backing Mussolini.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With vegetables, obviously' is a further hint: produce is also fruit and vegetables collectively.
explanation.definitionFit: To produce a play is to stage it, putting it on for an audience.

clue.text: A person of a foreign land is not exactly real with one.

definitions.text: A person of a foreign land

indicators.note: not exactly means the letters of real are not in their exact order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A foreigner is not quite genuine, along with someone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' looks like a verb but is taken as written; 'not exactly' gives RAEL.
explanation.definitionFit: An Israeli is a citizen of Israel, a person from another country to the American setter.

clue.text: Often trees have part of the meal to show for it.

indicators.note: the two words have the answer within them, spanning the break between them

parts.note: the end of 'often' and the start of 'trees' together spell the course

explanation.surface: Orchard trees often yield some of the dinner as a result.
explanation.walkthrough: 'have' says the words contain the answer, which runs across the end of 'often' and most of 'trees'.
explanation.definitionFit: An entree is a course of a meal: the main course in American usage, a dish before it in British.

clue.text: Benedict Arnold, for example, turning green with drink.

indicators.note: turning means the letters of green change into a new arrangement

parts.note: ade is a fruit drink such as lemonade, used alone in crosswords

explanation.surface: The famous traitor goes green after a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' turns GREEN into RENEG. Benedict Arnold was the American Revolutionary general who defected to the British.
explanation.definitionFit: Arnold is America's archetypal traitor, and a renegade is one who deserts a cause for the other side.
